summary.text: A lovely nymph of Aonia whom the river Cephisus entwined in his winding stream; she bore Narcissus, already surpassingly beautiful at birth, and asked Tiresias whether the boy would live to old age.

story.text: Ovid makes her the first to test Tiresias' fateful prophecies. The caerulean nymph Liriope came with her son, fifteen years old and already a wonder to the nymphs, whom she had borne where the green merge of Cephissus' stream meets the land — the mighty river-god whom she declared the father of her boy. She implored the seer to say whether Narcissus would reach old age; he answered that he would, if he never recognized himself.

Her story lives on the Metamorphoses shelf as `narcissus-echo`, where pride and Nemesis' answer prove the prophecy; Hyginus and Pausanias name only the river Cephisus as Narcissus' father, but Ovid gives the mother her name and her place beside the Boeotian water.
